Eadweard Muybridge. A British photographer famous for pioneering motion photography—using sequences of rapid sequential photographs to decompose and analyse movement. His work in the eighteen seventies and eighties bridged still photography and cinema, revealing the mechanics of animal and human locomotion in unprecedented detail.

In 1877 and 1878 Muybridge conducted the famous horse-in-motion experiment, commissioned by Leland Stanford to settle a bet. The question was simple: are all four hooves of a galloping horse airborne simultaneously? The answer was yes. The series of photographs shocked the art world and contradicted centuries of painted convention about how horses actually move. He created Animal Locomotion in 1887, an encyclopedia of seven hundred and eighty-one sequential photographs of humans and animals in motion—walking, running, jumping, climbing, dancing—arranged in high-speed sequences.

Muybridge invented an early form of motion-picture technology by printing sequential photos on a spinning disc he called the zoopraxiscope. When rotated before a light source, it created the illusion of continuous motion, functioning as a precursor to cinema. His motion studies revolutionised scientific understanding of anatomy and biomechanics. Artists, dancers, and engineers studied his plates to understand how bodies actually move versus how tradition had depicted them.

Muybridge pursued scientific documentation while his contemporary Alfred Stieglitz focused on aesthetic and fine-art concerns. Later photographer Ansel Adams inherited from Muybridge a rigorous experimental approach to light and technical mastery of exposure and printing. Dorothea Lange's Depression-era social-realist photographs also pursued truth through careful sequential composition.
